title: FLASHBACK: The Kingfish as a poltergeist?
excerpt: From legislative debates to spooky sightings at the Hilton, learn how the spirit of Huey Long continues to haunt Louisiana.
content:
When Louisiana politicos talk about the “ghost of Huey Long,” they’re often speaking metaphorically about the shadow his legacy (for better or worse) still casts over the state, and not just from the statue of him that gazes on the Capitol he built.

“Exorcising the ghost of Huey Long” was a recurring theme as lawmakers struggled to balance the budget, WRKF reported (opens wrkf.org in a new tab) on Halloween 2017.

“Huey wanted the power focused on Baton Rouge,” said former Sen. Conrad Appel, now on the Board of Elementary and Secondary Education. “He wanted the ability to micromanage what happens in the local parishes and cities, and that was his way of doing it, because anybody that controls the money controls the power.”

Dead or alive, the former governor and U.S. senator has long been a popular boogeyman for conservatives. In a 2023 column, Jeff Crouere lamented that “the ghost of Huey Long has been haunting the state ever since the 1930's,” blaming him for a “socialist mentality.” In 2019, Congressman Steve Scalise told an Illinois GOP audience that “the ghost of Huey Long still walks the State Capitol in Baton Rouge.”

But what about Huey’s actual ghost? He was mortally wounded at the Capitol, so it’s surprising there aren’t more stories about him haunting the state government skyscraper. One website (opens onlyinyourstate.com in a new tab) claims “many people believe that the Louisiana State Capitol building is haunted by the ghost of Sen. Huey P. Long,” though it doesn’t quote any of those people.

"Whenever things go missing around here, we blame it on Huey's ghost,” said Brenda Hodge, a radio correspondent and Senate staffer, in a “Folklife in Louisiana” piece (opens louisianafolklife.org in a new tab). “'I can't find that folder!' 'That's Huey's ghost.' Nobody's ever seen the ghost – well, nobody sober's ever seen the ghost – but that's what we say."

Sergeant at Arms Rhoda Verret said she experienced unexplained noise, sulfuric odor and generally weird vibes late at night in Alario Hall, according to a Manship School News Service report that ran in The (Houma) Courier in 2016. She also spotted, on surveillance footage, a gentleman in a white coat and pants standing near the governor’s and speaker’s parking spots looking out toward the lake.

“I left to go approach him to see if I could help him with something or give him directions, because he looked as if he was looking for something, and when I got there, he was gone,” Verret said. A coworker told her the description sounded more like another dead man: Long’s alleged assassin, Dr. Carl Weiss.

The Hilton Baton Rouge Capitol Center, known as the Heidelberg in Long’s day, was one of Huey’s favorite haunts in life and purportedly (opens theadvocate.com in a new tab) in death. In 1992, The Advocate published a story about workers for Pentagon Petroleum, which owned the then-shuttered hotel, spotting his ghost wandering a hallway during a routine building check. They also claimed to occasionally hear piano music coming from the ballroom; maybe Long and his hand-picked LSU bandleader Castro Carazo were working on another fight song (opens louisianamusichalloffame.org in a new tab).

And it has been said (opens historichotels.org in a new tab) that Long haunts the Hilton’s 10th floor. Though the hotel has been smoke-free since 2006, housekeepers have reported leaving rooms they've just cleaned and catching a whiff of cigar smoke, perhaps wafting from Huey’s spectral stogie.

*** This history feature was first published on Oct. 29, 2026, in Issue 1532 of LaPolitics Weekly. Wish you would have read it then? Subscribe today!
